column1: In Logic Pro's Project Settings > Audio, what bit depth should you always record at, and why?
column2: 24-bit, because it gives ~144 dB of dynamic range so a passage recorded too low still has usable resolution instead of audible quantization noise; you only bounce down to 16-bit at final delivery.

column1: What input peak range (in dBFS) should you target while recording in Logic Pro, and why can't you fix it later?
column2: -18 dBFS to -6 dBFS. Digital clipping at 0 dBFS is a hard, unrecoverable ceiling (unlike analog tape saturation), so this gain-staging decision can't be undone with EQ or compression afterward.

column1: What I/O Buffer Size should you use while tracking vs. while mixing in Logic Pro, and why?
column2: 32–64 samples while tracking (lowest latency so a performer hears themselves without delay, but higher CPU load); 256–512+ samples while mixing (stable processing headroom since latency doesn't matter with no live input).

column1: Why should you avoid changing a Logic Pro project's sample rate mid-project?
column2: It forces a sample-rate conversion on every existing audio file in the project, which should be avoided — confirm sample rate and bit depth before the first take.

column1: In MIDI, what do the three bytes of a Note On message represent, and what does a Note On with velocity 0 mean?
column2: Status byte (90 = Note On, channel 1), note number, and velocity. A Note On with velocity 0 is treated as a Note Off, which is why recorded MIDI data sometimes shows no explicit Note Off message.

column1: What is the 'octave naming trap' in Logic Pro MIDI, and why does it matter?
column2: Logic names MIDI note 60 as C3, while many other DAWs call it C4 (or even C5). If a patch 'plays an octave off' after import/export between DAWs, check this naming convention before troubleshooting further.

column1: What do CC64 values 0–63 and 64–127 mean in Logic Pro MIDI?
column2: CC64 is the sustain pedal: values 0–63 mean pedal off (up), values 64–127 mean pedal on (down).

column1: What is Logic Pro's timeline tick resolution, and what is one tick's duration at 100 BPM?
column2: 960 ticks per quarter note. At 100 BPM, one tick = 0.625 ms.

column1: What is the key difference between a Summing Stack and a Folder Stack in Logic Pro?
column2: A Summing Stack routes sub-tracks to one new summing channel strip with its own fader and inserts (sub-faders become relative to it). A Folder Stack is purely a visual/organizational container — sub-tracks remain independently routed to the main output, with no new summing channel created.

column1: How can you test whether you built a Summing Stack vs. a Folder Stack in Logic Pro?
column2: Solo the stack's header track. If the sub-tracks mute too (because they feed the sum), it's a Summing Stack. If soloing the parent does nothing (children are independently routed to Stereo Out), it's a Folder Stack.

column1: In Logic Pro mixing, why does compressor attack time change a sound's perceived punch and sustain?
column2: Fast attack tames transients, reducing punch and increasing perceived sustain loudness. Slow attack lets transients through, increasing punch with more pronounced 'duck and recover' dynamics — the compressor is dividing time between a sound's attack (rhythmic clarity) and sustain (tonal body/loudness).

column1: What is the formula for approximate round-trip audio latency in Logic Pro, and what does it reveal about the buffer size tradeoff?
column2: Round-trip latency (ms) ≈ (Buffer Size / Sample Rate) × 2 × 1000. Small buffer = low latency but little headroom for plugin processing per block; large buffer = high latency but much more DSP headroom.
